The short answer is that I can vote. Feel free to join the "voting doesn't matter" chorus if you like, but it's a cynical argument that doesn't hold water. In any case, "voting with your wallet" only matters in a very limited set of circumstances that seem important but aren't. Choosing whether you buy your gas from a BP or Shell station might feel like an important decision, but the truly important decisions (who heats your home, who builds your roads, who constructs our absurd military arsenal) are all out of your hands.

A better answer is this: the government is the only entity that doesn't have to make a profit. There are certainly some things that private companies can do better than the government, but there are many important things the government is forced to do because they would be a waste of time and money for any profitable enterprise. Regulation is a perfect example; it's always cheaper for companies to cut corners than do what's best for the public. A for-profit regulatory agency would simply take bribes from the corner-cutting companies and ignore the public, who couldn't afford to pay them any better. Education is another endeavor that's a tremendous waste of money from a business perspective. Private schools often do a good job of educating a small group of paying students whom they can pick and choose. If you have the money and you pass the entry tests, you can have the privilege of paying for your education. Unfortunately, the vast majority of students don't qualify, so the government has to pay for the rest of the kids. Can you imagine a for-profit school exclusively for special needs children? How could it possibly make money?

Anyway, the word "trust" is a bit of a stretch. I think it's easier to hold the government accountable than a private business, although that accountability gets more elusive every day thanks to the efforts of those same businesses. The problem with free market capitalism is that it, and it's associated theories, are based on an enlightened self interest. Most often, people acting in the moment seem to act in astonishing ignorance of the long term effects of their personal decisions. Group dissociation from responsibility for decisions compounds this effect even more. See the constantly repeated studies where people behave in ways exactly contrary to best practices according to game theory. Simply put, we aren't smart enough to make personal decisions in the group's best interest, because we are too short sighted and reactionary.

In addition, you have the social effect of modern corporations. In previous times, a shop owner, etc would have at least a personal accountability to the customers they served because they would live in the same community and suffer the same effects of their decisions as their customer base. Now, that is the exception not the rule. Also, modern corporations are so large and respond to boards requests not individuals requests that there is often no individual accountability for actions taken by a corporation. This removes yet another social protection against both corporate misuse of resources and outright malicious action on the part of corporations,.

Taken together, along with the continued evidence of corporations acting in bad faith in regards to their customer base, let alone anyone who doesn't fall in their customer base and are only bystanders (citizens of countries where resource harvesting take place, etc), and the educated person comes to the conclusion that you can not rely on corporations to self regulate.

Now, in my opinion, they fail to realize that governments too seem to act in bad faith, but if you leave off reliance on for profit corporations, you are left with only non-profits (many of which have all but corporate power structures regardless of their tax classification), or the government of the citizens involved. And the fact is, if you acknowledge that governments are also morally bankrupt in different but practically similar ways, you're left with a frightening landscape where there is no apparent recourse for harms done by anyone. So they cling to the idea that governments are the answer, because currently they are the only answer, even though in practice they are as inneffective as the corporations they are supposed to regulate.

That being said, it should be the governments who regulate and prevent harms from corporations (and indeed all groups and individuals who would harm people). That is the whole purpose of governments, from monarchies and tribal structures up through modern representative democracies. One of the biggest barriers to a true free market is the public's lack of complete information. Say a fracking company has two chemicals they could include along with the water they inject into the ground. They both serve the same purpose except one costs half as much as the other and produces an additional 20% yield of usable gas. Unfortunately, it's also a known carcinogen and the public would refuse to allow the chemical to be injected into their aquifers ... if they knew it was being used. It's not more cost-effective for the company to use a safer chemical and they're not required to disclose to the public what chemicals they use, so why would they do the right thing?

If it weren't for government regulations (admittedly weak due to regulatory capture) and the ability of citizens to sue the company in a government court (although the compensation is limited thanks to corporate lobbying for tort reforms), the free market would fail them completely. They would have no recourse in that situation except to filter their water (just kidding, a Brita filter doesn't remove chemical pollutants).

The government interferes with prices in a way that is less than ideal because there are other concerns that have to be addressed. Sometimes that interference is negative (for instance, the Endangered Species Act is very easily abused to prevent people from using certain lands for legitimate purposes), but it's often beneficial. The government is required to publicly release laws, financial information, and Congressional votes so that people can make informed decisions, whereas private companies can keep their entire operation secret. Expecting a company to make a decision that benefits the public at a greater expense to themselves is the worst kind of "trust" you can have, and blaming the government for the those decisions (somehow) is a non-sequitor.

Liberal here. Saying we trust the government over a corporation is a gross oversimplification. I don't trust either the government (either of the two ruling parties) or corporations. This is the case for most people who are even remotely interested in politics.

When I say that I want an expansion of government's role in society, I don't say that as a blanket statement referring to a general growth of all aspects of our government. I look at issues on a case-by-case basis. I think that government serves a different purpose than a corporation, and there are certain activities that are currently relegated to the private sector that would be better served by the government.

For example, I think internet should be provided by the government as a utility. The point of having a free market is to increase market efficiency by forcing firms to compete and allowing that competition to filter out market inefficiency through failure. Internet service is a natural monopoly, and the resulting lack of competition removes the benefit provided by allowing a free market for that sector. There is a reason Comcast has shitty customer service, and it's the same reason our government often provides shitty customer service: there is no accountability for them. They have a monopoly, so they don't have to provide good customer service.

That being said, I am a liberal in the US. If I lived anywhere else in the western world I would probably be considered a conservative. But here, I'm about as far left as it gets.

For example, I think internet should be provided by the government as a utility.

This would be an unmitigated disaster for so many reasons, starting with the fact that the NSA would absolutely love a fully public-sector Internet and that the government could easily censor content that criticizes them. And one look at how existing government services work should disabuse you of the notion that a government-run Internet would be cheaper, more efficient, or more consumer-friendly.

It's also worth noting that the dawn of the modern Internet didn't come about until after ARPANET was declassified in the late '70s (allowing commercial networks to connect to it, soon greatly exceeding the number of military networks on it) and formally expired in 1989, and it didn't become popular until after the NSF privatized the Internet's backbone in 1994. Nearly every major innovation on the Internet has come from the private sector as a direct result of the government getting out. Put them in charge again and innovation will come to a screeching halt.
